P1_fx_receipts.question: Can resident individuals receive foreign currency for services or digital exports? Any conversion or repatriation rule?
P1_fx_receipts.answer: Yes, with no exchange controls. Kenya repealed the Exchange Control Act effective 27 December 1995, and FX business was delegated to authorised dealers. Foreign currency received can be credited to a foreign-currency account, sold to an authorised dealer, used to settle external obligations, or used to settle local debts billed in foreign currency. Residents may invoice in shillings or foreign currency. Dealers must obtain and keep documents for transactions above US$10,000; declaration forms are accepted where e-banking is used.

sources.quote: It may be noted that the responsibility of managing foreign exchange business was delegated to the authorised foreign exchange dealers following repeal of the Exchange Control Act effective December 27, 1995.

sources.title: Guidelines on Foreign Exchange

P2_fcy_account.question: Can individuals hold a foreign-currency bank account?
P2_fcy_account.answer: Yes. With exchange controls repealed since 1995, foreign currency received may be credited to a foreign-currency account (CBK guidelines). The guidelines state explicitly that authorised banks are free to open FCY accounts for certain categories (diplomatic missions, forex bureaus). A general statement on ordinary resident individuals' FCY accounts was not found in the text read.

P3_local_gateways.question: Licensed local online payment gateways, and whether individuals or sole proprietors can sign up
P3_local_gateways.answer: Global platform availability for Kenya (automated collector snapshots, Oct 2026). Available: Stripe (merchant sign-up); Paddle (not on its exclusion list; software sellers only, each seller reviewed); Lemon Squeezy (bank payouts); Polar (payouts); Whop (payouts); Google Play (developer registration); YouTube Partner Program. Not listed: Dodo Payments (sellers); Etsy seller payments.

P4_paypal.question: PayPal capability in the country
P4_paypal.answer: PayPal works in Kenya: the Payouts table lists Kenya as 'Send, receive, and withdraw'. Withdrawals go to a bank (Wallet then 'Transfer to your bank'), or to M-PESA through Safaricom's PayPal service. That service moves funds between your own PayPal and M-PESA accounts in USD only, converts to KES, charges 3% of the applicable forex rate plus Safaricom C2B charges, and needs an Android device.

L1_registration.question: Must an individual selling digital products or services register a business? How (sole proprietor), cost, online?
L1_registration.answer: Sole proprietorships are registered with the Business Registration Service (BRS) under the Registration of Business Names Act. Guides say this applies when you trade under a name different from your own personal name. Registration is online via eCitizen (BRS), with name reservation and registration merged into one step, and the government fee is KES 950. A KRA PIN (L2) is needed regardless. A county Single Business Permit is also mentioned by one guide as mandatory before operating (NOT verified).

L1_registration.notes: The Act's text (kenyalaw.org) was unreachable, so the 'name different from your own' trigger rests on secondary guides; one older document (AMK Africa) says registration is not legally required. County Single Business Permits (Nairobi etc.) were not researched; they may apply to home-based or online businesses. Kenzobe's tax lines (TOT 1% under 5M) are outdated and were not used.

L2_tax_id.question: Tax identification number requirement and how to get it
L2_tax_id.answer: The KRA PIN (Personal Identification Number), used for dealings with KRA, other government agencies and various service providers. Individuals register online on iTax (itax.kra.go.ke). Every individual with a KRA PIN must file an annual return by 30 June, even with no income (KRA, per search summary). Paystack's Registered Business tier requires a KRA PIN.

L3_income_tax_foreign.question: How residents' foreign-sourced or digital income is taxed
L3_income_tax_foreign.answer: Kenya taxes income accrued in or derived from Kenya (Income Tax Act s.3). KRA's example: a computer programmer in Kenya giving IT consultancy to an offshore company earns that income in Kenya, so it is taxable in Kenya. Freelance work done from Kenya for foreign clients is therefore taxable. Exceptions also tax some foreign income: foreign employment income of residents, and business carried on partly outside Kenya. Small businesses: Turnover Tax at 1.5% of gross sales (since 1 July 2023) is a FINAL tax for residents with turnover above KES 1,000,000 and not above KES 25,000,000. There are no deductions, simplified records, filing and payment through iTax, and no year-end income tax return on that income.

L3_income_tax_foreign.notes: CONFLICT inside KRA sources: the TOT page body says KES 1m-25m, but (per a search summary) its introduction says KES 50m, and the 2021 revised Income Tax Act says 50m. The 25m figure matches the Finance Act 2023 era and is used; confirm with KRA. Slab income-tax rates and the 2025/2026 Finance Acts were not checked. Whether a resident freelancer can choose TOT for foreign-client service income was not confirmed. A KRA blog says residents are taxed on worldwide income, which conflicts with the source-based FAQ; the FAQ plus the s.3 example are used.

L4_vat_gst.question: VAT/GST rate, registration threshold, treatment of exported services and digital services
L4_vat_gst.answer: VAT Act 2013: general rate 16%; 0% on certain supplies including exports — and since 1 July 2023 (Finance Act 2023) the exportation of taxable SERVICES is zero-rated again (it was 16% from July 2022 to June 2023, except BPO), with refunds of input tax for zero-rated suppliers. You must register once taxable supplies reach or are expected to reach KES 5 million in a year (KRA brochure, reviewed October 2024).

L5_data_protection.question: Data-protection law: name, year, in force?, regulator
L5_data_protection.answer: Data Protection Act 2019, enforced by the Office of the Data Protection Commissioner (ODPC). Data controllers and processors must register with ODPC. You are exempt from mandatory registration if annual turnover or revenue is below KES 5 million AND you have fewer than 10 employees, unless you process data for Third Schedule purposes (e.g. political canvassing, crime prevention/CCTV, gambling, education, health). Exempt entities must still comply with Parts IV and VI of the Act (principles and data-subject rights).

L6_consumer_ecommerce.question: E-commerce / consumer-protection law relevant to online sales
L6_consumer_ecommerce.answer: The Competition Authority of Kenya (CAK) enforces consumer protection under the Competition Act (CAP 504), including preventing misleading market conduct, and the Constitution grants consumer rights. The Consumer Protection Act 2012 also exists, but its text (Kenya Law) was unreachable, so e-commerce-specific duties such as distance-selling cancellation rights were NOT verified.

D1_id_document.answer: The Kenyan National ID card. Its third generation is the 'Maisha card', piloted from 2024 and tied to the lifelong Maisha Namba number. It is issued by the National Registration Bureau. Paystack accepts a national ID or valid passport.

W1_workarounds.question: Simple, legal routes around payment barriers for a beginner (no misrepresentation, nominees or sanctions evasion)
W1_workarounds.answer: Barriers: none of the major platform barriers apply. Simple legal routes: (1) Sell digital products or software through a merchant of record: Paddle (software/SaaS only; each seller reviewed), Lemon Squeezy (bank payouts), Polar. The platform is the legal seller to your customers, handles card payments and consumer VAT/sales tax, and pays you out. You still declare the payouts as your income at home (see L3). (2) Sell services on Upwork, which is available here (not on its restricted list). Which withdrawal methods you get (bank, PayPal, Payoneer, etc.) depends on the country and shows in your account. (3) Creator income through the YouTube Partner Program (available here). (4) Paid apps and in-app sales through Google Play (merchant registration available here). (5) Client payments by PayPal (on PayPal's Payouts list as 'Send, receive, and withdraw'). (6) Card payments on your own site through Paystack (a Stripe company). Stripe lists this country under its extended network. (7) For direct clients, a bank transfer (SWIFT) into your own local account always works. Follow the local foreign-exchange rules (see P1) and keep invoices. (8) Local official channel: There are no exchange controls; foreign currency can be credited to a foreign-currency account at a Kenyan bank (P1/P2). Avoid: opening accounts with a foreign address, a relative's or friend's identity, or a VPN to look like you are elsewhere. It breaches platform terms (accounts and funds get frozen) and can break anti-money-laundering or sanctions law.
